description: Machine-readable evidence for the Web Fleet integration boundary: the deliberately defined API-token surface (also mirrored in route-inventory.json tokenScopes) and the webhook outbox/delivery contract. Tests live in internal/server/token_test.go, internal/apitokens/tokens_test.go and internal/notifications/webhook_test.go.

apiTokenSurface.authentication: Authorization: Bearer <token> on routes that declare a token scope; routes without a token scope are session-only and a token cannot reach them.
apiTokenSurface.identity: The acting organization is the token's organization, fixed at creation. A token cannot cross organization boundaries and cannot inherit the creator's role or browser session privileges: its authorization is exactly its scopes.
apiTokenSurface.abuseProtection: Failed/malformed Bearer authentication is throttled per trusted-proxy-resolved client address with a bounded-memory fixed window, so spoofed X-Forwarded-For cannot bypass it and successful high-volume API use is not throttled. Rate-limit keys are client addresses, never token prefixes or raw token values.
guarantees: malformed and unknown tokens denied with a generic error (no existence oracle)
revoked tokens denied with the same generic error
no CSRF required for token-authenticated mutations (the bearer credential is the CSRF control)
error responses are exactly one JSON document (single response owner)
token secret returned only at creation and stored only as a SHA-256 hash
revocation scoped to the token's owner and organization

webhooks.organizationIsolation: A delivery row is enqueued only for enabled webhooks belonging to the incident site's own organization, derived from the persisted site inside the same transaction. An incident in organization A can never queue a payload to organization B's webhooks, and a disabled webhook never receives an event.
webhooks.outbox: Incident transitions commit the incident state and insert pending delivery rows for enabled same-organization webhooks in the same transaction (payload_json attached). Delivery never runs in the transition path, so a slow or malicious webhook cannot block monitoring or incident state.
webhooks.delivery: A background worker processes pending rows with bounded retries (3), bounded timeout (8s), bounded response bodies (64KiB) and a global concurrency limit (2). 3xx responses are treated as failures because redirects are never followed.
webhooks.signature: Header X-WebFleet-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, exact delivered body)>. The body is built once per delivery and reused across retries so every retry signs the exact payload being delivered.
webhooks.duplicateBehavior: At-least-once: a crash between enqueue and final status leaves the row pending and it is reprocessed, which can duplicate delivery. The delivered envelope carries a stable event_id (the delivery row id) as the receiver's deduplication identity; sent_at may differ across reprocessing, so the signature alone is not a stable dedup key.
webhooks.ssrf: Destinations must be HTTPS and resolve to a public address at creation (netguard). Delivery uses the guarded dialer, which re-resolves the full answer set at dial time and fails closed on any blocked address or mixed public/private answer, so localhost, private, link-local, cloud-metadata and rebinding targets are unreachable even from a tampered row.
webhooks.singleBoundary: notifications.Service.Deliver (the old synchronous unguarded delivery path) has been removed. The background worker is the only webhook delivery boundary; a future caller of a removed symbol cannot compile, preventing silent reintroduction of direct synchronous webhook HTTP.
webhooks.secrets: Webhook secrets are cryptographically random, returned only at creation, and stored plaintext at rest because the worker must recover them to produce HMAC signatures. This is a documented threat-model decision: webhook secrets are not hashed like API tokens. Delivery errors are redacted and never include secrets or response bodies.
